bull.b: Recurring revenue growth makes the business less dependent on one-time instrument sales and increases the value of each installed system over time. As utilization expands across 169 validated systems, consumables and service revenue can provide a more durable base for future growth.

Strong consumables growth indicates customers are using the platform in routine testing workflows rather than treating it as a one-time equipment purchase. This recurring pull-through can deepen customer relationships, improve revenue visibility, and support increasing contribution from the installed base.

The sharp improvement in gross and service margins shows progress in cost structure, service productivity, and manufacturing efficiency. If sustained as placements and consumable volumes grow, better margins could improve the economics of the installed base and move the company closer to eventual cash-flow breakeven.

bear.b: Large continuing losses show that revenue growth has not yet translated into operating leverage or financial self-sufficiency. Until expenses scale more effectively, the company may need to preserve cash or obtain additional funding, limiting its flexibility to invest through periods of slower execution.

Persistent negative cash generation means reported growth and improving gross margins are not yet funding the business internally. Continued cash consumption can constrain investment choices and increase dependence on financing, particularly while the company remains far from reported operating breakeven.

Rising leverage alongside declining equity and assets reduces balance-sheet flexibility while losses continue. The company’s plans also involve accessing future debt tranches and potential warrant proceeds, so financing availability and execution against milestones remain important to sustaining operations and growth.
